summary: Specifies DNS64, which creates AAAA records from A records so IPv6-only clients can reach IPv4-only servers through a translator. It also gives deployment suggestions. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: DNS64 creates an IPv6-form address from an IPv4 address when a DNS lookup finds no usable AAAA record. An IPv6-only client can then send traffic to a translator that connects it to the IPv4 server.

questions: synthesize aaaa records from a records
how does dns64 synthesize aaaa records
where can the dns64 function run
subtitle: How DNS64 gives IPv6-only clients synthesized addresses for IPv4-only servers.

tldr.problem: An IPv6-only client may need to contact an IPv4-only server by name, but the server has no IPv6 address record for the client to use.
tldr.mechanism: DNS64 first looks for an AAAA record. If none is usable, it looks up A records and synthesizes AAAA records by embedding each IPv4 address in a configured IPv6 prefix understood by a translator.
tldr.outcome: With a compatible IPv6/IPv4 translator, the client can initiate communication without changes to either host. DNS64 changes DNS answers, so its interaction with DNSSEC and multihomed hosts needs care.

today: RFC 6147 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it specifies DNS64 for use with an IPv6/IPv4 translator such as RFC 6146.

sections.title: The Problem DNS64 Solves
sections.content:
DNS64 is a DNS function for IPv4/IPv6 transition. Used with an IPv6/IPv4 translator, it lets an IPv6-only client start communication by name with an IPv4-only server.

It synthesizes an AAAA record from an A record. The synthesized record keeps the A record's name but carries an IPv6 address created from the IPv4 address and configured parameters, usually an IPv6 prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: An IPv6-only client cannot directly use an IPv4 address record. DNS64 creates an IPv6-form address that the configured translator can map to the server's IPv4 address.

sections.title: How DNS64 and the Translator Work Together
sections.content:
DNS64 receives a request for an AAAA record and first looks for real AAAA data. If no usable record exists, it looks up A records and creates a synthetic AAAA record for each result.

The DNS64 function and translator must use the same address-generation algorithm and prefix. Packets addressed to that prefix must reach a translator configured for it. The RFC describes a Well-Known Prefix and Network-Specific Prefixes.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS64 and the translator use matching rules to represent an IPv4 address inside an IPv6 address. The network routes that address to the translator, which can then reach the IPv4 server.

sections.title: Where the DNS64 Function Can Run
sections.content:
The DNS64 function can run in an authoritative server, a recursive resolver, or a host's stub resolver. In recursive-resolver mode, existing IPv6 nodes can use it without modification. Stub-resolver mode needs changes to the host but can work with DNSSEC validation performed there.

In all placements, the DNS64 and translator need matching configuration. The function appears to a client as a DNS server or resolver.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS64 can run in a DNS server or in the client device. Running it in a recursive resolver avoids changing existing clients, while running it in the host supports host-side DNSSEC validation.

sections.title: Answering an AAAA Query
sections.content:
For an Internet-class AAAA query, DNS64 first retrieves real AAAA records. By default, it MUST NOT synthesize records when real, non-excluded AAAA data exists. If the answer is empty, DNS64 asks for A records and can synthesize an AAAA answer from them.

The synthetic record uses the A record's name, type 28, class 1, and an RDLENGTH of 16. Its TTL is the minimum of relevant source TTLs; if the negative answer provides no SOA record, DNS64 SHOULD use the A-record TTL or 600 seconds, whichever is shorter.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS64 uses a real IPv6 record when one is available. Only when the answer is empty does it look up an IPv4 record and create a synthetic IPv6 answer.

sections.title: Generating an IPv6 Representation
sections.content:
The address-generation algorithm MUST be the same at DNS64 and at the translator, and it MUST be reversible so the IPv4 address can be recovered. Its inputs are limited to the IPv4 address, the configured prefix, and optional stable parameters configured at both places.

Each prefix length must be no greater than 96. DNS64 MUST support the algorithm in RFC 6052, and that algorithm is the default. If no prefix is configured, the RFC specifies the Well-Known Prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: The DNS64 and translator use the same reversible recipe to build and read the IPv6 representation. A mismatch in the recipe or prefix prevents the address from leading to the intended IPv4 destination.

sections.title: Deployment and DNSSEC Considerations
sections.content:
A synthetic address is specific to the network and translator configuration that created it. A multihomed host may receive an answer on one network and try to use it on another, where no matching translator is available. Hosts with native IPv4 may also send traffic through NAT64 when native IPv4 would be preferable.

DNS64 changes DNS answers, while DNSSEC detects changes. A validating DNS64 must validate the negative AAAA response before querying for A data. When the query has both CD and DO set, it MUST NOT synthesize; the client must perform validation and synthesis itself.
sections.plainLanguage: A synthesized address works only where its matching translator is reachable. DNSSEC validation also needs to account for DNS64, because synthesis changes the answer the client receives.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An attacker who changes the prefix used by DNS64 can direct client traffic to a different destination. The RFC identifies possible denial of service, unwanted traffic to other devices, or eavesdropping if the altered prefix routes through the attacker.

DNS64 deployments need consistent prefix configuration and DNSSEC behavior appropriate to where validation occurs. A validator unaware of DNS64 may treat synthesized data as modified and reject it.
sections.plainLanguage: The prefix is part of the route to the translator, so changing it can send traffic to the wrong place. DNSSEC validators must also understand whether DNS64 has changed a DNS answer.
